Primary user: Business users, analysts, and data teams already using Databricks
Primary use case: Ask natural-language questions over governed Databricks data and receive SQL-backed answers, tables, visualizations, and follow-up analysis
Key strength: Deep integration with Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, dashboards, applications, and agent workflows
Key weakness: Reliable use requires curated views, detailed instructions, trusted examples, testing, and ongoing review
Evidence: Direct teardown evidence: 30-question benchmark average 7.87/10; 24/30 answers were numerically correct, but only 18/30 fully followed business definitions. The targeted retest improved selected questions from 5.73/10 to 7.91/10, while three questions regressed. Official documentation supports Unity Catalog governance, generated SQL, editable visualizations, monitoring, benchmarks, trusted assets, and conversation/management APIs.
Notes: Only product in this comparison tested directly. Setup effort score is inverse: 5 means easiest setup and 1 means heaviest setup.

Product category: Cloud data warehouse-native natural-language analytics service
Primary user: Business users, analytics engineers, data teams, and application developers using Snowflake
Primary use case: Translate natural-language questions into SQL using governed Semantic Views, verified queries, and custom business instructions
Key strength: Strong semantic governance, verified queries, SQL transparency, monitoring, and built-in evaluation with regression tracking
Key weakness: Requires a well-designed Semantic View and offers a less complete visualization experience than BI-native products
Evidence: Official documentation shows schema-level Semantic Views with metrics, relationships, synonyms, and custom instructions; a Verified Query Repository; generated SQL, warnings, and confidence metadata; administrator monitoring; and evaluations that compare generated SQL with verified queries while tracking accuracy, regressions, and latency. The REST API supports multi-turn conversations and application integration.
Notes: Scored from official documentation, not a hands-on benchmark. Several optimization and evaluation capabilities remain preview features.

Primary user: Business users, BI teams, data engineers, and organizations using Fabric, Power BI, or Microsoft Copilot
Primary use case: Ask natural-language questions across Fabric warehouses, lakehouses, semantic models, KQL data, ontologies, graph data, and other connected sources
Key strength: Broad data-source coverage, Power BI semantic-model support, evaluation SDK, diagnostics, Git integration, and deployment pipelines
Key weakness: The experience spans many configuration layers, and several advanced capabilities are still in preview
Evidence: Official Microsoft documentation supports SQL, DAX, KQL, graph, ontology, mirrored database, and search sources; agent-level and data-source instructions; example queries; ground-truth evaluation with the Fabric Data Agent SDK; downloadable diagnostics; Git and deployment-pipeline lifecycle management; visual responses; external SDK access; and integrations with Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Foundry, and MCP.
Notes: Scored from official documentation. Core query tooling is available, but visual responses, evaluation, some integrations, and creator assistance include preview elements.

Primary user: Business users, analysts, product teams, and organizations prioritizing self-service analytics
Primary use case: Ask multi-step analytical questions, verify the logic through search tokens, build visual answers, and trigger business workflows
Key strength: Business-user-focused conversational analytics with verifiable search tokens, a governed semantic layer, strong visualization, and embedded workflow actions
Key weakness: The strongest reliability claims come mainly from vendor documentation and were not independently benchmarked in this teardown
Evidence: ThoughtSpot describes Spotter as a multi-step analytics agent that uses governed search tokens instead of direct text-to-SQL. Spotter Semantics defines business logic, metrics, joins, calendars, and security rules. SpotterViz supports natural-language dashboard creation, while connectors and embedded workflows can send results to tools such as Slack, Jira, and Salesforce. ThoughtSpot's setup guide states that a focused initial setup can be completed in roughly one to two hours, while still requiring a prepared semantic model and validation by power users.
Notes: Highest provisional score, but based on vendor documentation and product claims rather than direct testing. Requires validation in a controlled benchmark.

Product category: BI-native visual analytics and authoring assistant
Primary user: Dashboard consumers, analysts, and Tableau authors
Primary use case: Explore data, create visualizations and calculations, and summarize or question existing dashboards through natural language
Key strength: Strongest visual-analysis, dashboard-authoring, sharing, and embedding experience in the comparison
Key weakness: Less focused on transparent governed natural-language-to-SQL analysis, and important dashboard-agent capabilities remain beta
Evidence: Official Tableau documentation shows that Tableau Agent can explore data, create visualizations, create and explain calculations, and provide dashboard overviews and insights. Tableau provides mature permissions and embedding APIs, including the ability to launch the analytics assistant in embedded views. However, dashboard Q&A and narratives are beta, setup requires Tableau AI licensing and permissions, and the product exposes less SQL-level transparency than Databricks or Snowflake.
Notes: Scored as an adjacent competitor rather than a pure natural-language-to-SQL agent. Underlying Tableau platform is mature, but some Agent dashboard features are beta.
